name: Fucoidan (brown seaweed polysaccharide)
short: Hepatitis B, 51 people, 48 weeks, no comparison group described: white cells, platelets, albumin fell. Liver cancer (82): adverse events like placebo, none severe. Clotting test longer, group unnamed.
text: Fucoidan is a sulfated polysaccharide extracted from brown seaweeds; these data are for fucoidan extracts, not whole seaweed or kelp. Where the abstracts give a route, fucoidan was taken by mouth; the others do not state one, and none of the cited abstracts mentions use on the skin. In a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 82 people with unresectable liver cancer having transarterial chemoembolisation, low-molecular-weight fucoidan for 6 months had adverse event rates similar to placebo, and no severe adverse events occurred. In a 12-week randomised placebo-controlled trial in 122 people with osteoarthritis of a Fucus vesiculosus extract (85% fucoidan), adverse events were closely monitored, blood tests of liver, kidney and blood-cell function showed no clinically significant changes, and the authors describe it as safe and well tolerated. In a placebo-controlled crossover trial in 16 active adults taking fucoidan from Undaria pinnatifida for 2 weeks, no adverse events were reported. On the other side, in a study of 51 people with chronic hepatitis B (the abstract describes no comparison group) in the immune tolerance phase who took oligo fucoidan for 48 weeks, white blood cell count, platelet count and albumin fell (P < 0.05); the abstract does not say whether these changes were clinically important. A 2022 systematic review of 4 studies (118 cancer patients) could not confirm cause and effect between fucoidan and adverse effects. Clotting: in a single-blinded pilot trial in 20 volunteers, 10 swallowed capsules of 75% fucoidan and 10 swallowed guar gum capsules for 12 days; the abstract reports that, in the body, the activated partial thromboplastin time (a clotting test) lengthened from 28.41 to 34.01 seconds and the thrombin time shortened from 18.62 to 17.55 seconds, each in 10 people, without naming their group. The authors concluded that fucoidan in that form does not seem to have an anticoagulant effect when taken by mouth, although it was strongly anticoagulant in laboratory tests; the abstract does not report on bleeding or other adverse events. In a study of 20 people who took mozuku fucoidan, up to 4.05 g a day for 2 weeks (described as an excessive intake), no disorder was apparent and blood and urine values stayed within normal ranges; the abstract describes no comparison group. Interactions: in an open-label study in 20 patients with breast cancer taking letrozole or tamoxifen (10 on each), 3 weeks of fucoidan from Undaria pinnatifida taken by mouth did not significantly change blood levels of these medicines or of tamoxifen's breakdown products, and no adverse effects of fucoidan were reported. No other interaction data were found in the cited sources.
